prompt: The `RunsOnce` button was clicked three times. How many lines of the transcript start with `render read count`?
hint: The first draw counts too.

prompt: In the `RunsOnce` demo, why does `setup ran` appear once although the button was clicked three times?
hint: Which part of the component is the render?

choices.text: `<script setup>` runs once, when the component is created
choices.why: Right. After that, only the render that read `count` runs again on each click.

choices.text: Vue prints a repeated console line once
choices.why: Nothing is merged: `render read count` was printed four times, one line per render.

choices.text: The inline handler `count++` bypasses the setup, and a named function would have run it again
choices.why: How the handler is written makes no difference. A change in Vue runs the renders that read the value, whatever wrote it.

choices.text: The setup ran on every click, but Vite's console shows a line from the setup only on the first load
choices.why: The transcript shows every line the page logged; `setup ran` is there once because the setup ran once.

prompt: A React component and a Vue component each log a line at the top of their code, outside anything rendered. The value they show changes three times. How many times is each line printed in all?
hint: In React, the whole function is the render.

choices.text: React 4, Vue 4
choices.why: That is the picture of Vue as React with different syntax. Vue's setup is not the render, and it does not run again.

choices.text: React 4, Vue 1
choices.why: Right. React calls the whole function for the first draw and for each change; Vue runs its setup once and reruns only the render.

choices.text: React 1, Vue 4
choices.why: The models are the other way round: React reruns the function, and Vue remembers what was read.

choices.text: React 3, Vue 3
choices.why: This forgets the first draw, and it treats the two models as one.

prompt: In `RunsOnce`, the button changes `count`. Which of these run again after a click? Choose all that apply.
hint: What did the template read?

choices.text: `console.log('setup ran')`
choices.why: It is in the setup, which ran once; the transcript shows it a single time.

choices.text: The template's render
choices.why: Right. It read `count`, so a write to `count` runs it again.

choices.text: The call to `ref(0)` that made `count`
choices.why: That would make a new ref at 0 on every click and the count would never grow. It belongs to the setup.

choices.text: `label()`, called from the template
choices.why: Right. The template calls it, so it runs every time the template does, and it logs each time.

prompt: With `const counts = { total: ref(0) }` in `<script setup>`, what did `{{ counts.total + 1 }}` show?
hint: `counts` is a plain object, and the ref is inside it.

choices.why: That is what `{{ total + 1 }}` showed, because `total` is a top-level name and was unwrapped before the `+`.

choices.text: `NaN`, because the `+` met an object it could not turn into a number
choices.why: When one side is an object, `+` turns it into a string and joins; it does not try for a number.

choices.text: `0`, because the interpolation unwrapped the ref and then ignored the addition
choices.why: That is `{{ counts.total }}` on its own. The unwrapping at the end happens after the `+` has already met the wrapper.

choices.text: `[object Object]1`
choices.why: Right. A ref nested in a plain object is not unwrapped inside an expression, so the `+` turned the wrapper into a string.

prompt: A helper `startTimer(m)` reads `m` once a minute and logs it. The component calls `startTimer(minutes.value)`, and later sets `minutes.value = 50`. What does the timer log after that?
hint: What was the helper handed: the wrapper, or what was inside it?

choices.text: 50, because a write to `.value` reaches everybody who read the ref
choices.why: The helper never read the ref. It was given the number that was inside it at that moment.

choices.text: The old number
choices.why: Right. `minutes.value` handed over a plain number, and a number does not change. Passing `minutes` itself would let the helper read the current value.

choices.text: A `RefImpl` object, because the ref is passed whole
choices.why: That is what passing `minutes` without `.value` would log. With `.value`, the number is passed.

choices.text: 50, once the update queue has run
choices.why: The queue reruns renders that read the ref. A function holding a copy of the number is not one of them.

prompt: For large data you replace whole and never change in place, `___` watches `.value` and nothing inside it.
hint: A variant of `ref`, named for how deep it looks.

prompt: In `ReactiveProxy`, the first click went through the proxy and the second added 10 to `raw.minutes`. What did the page say after both?
hint: `raw.minutes is now 50` was logged.

choices.text: spanish: 40 minutes
choices.why: Right. Only the first change went through the proxy, so only the first was seen.

choices.text: spanish: 50 minutes
choices.why: That is the value inside the object, but nothing told Vue it changed, so the page was not redrawn.

choices.text: spanish: 30 minutes
choices.why: The first click went through the proxy and was drawn: 30 became 40.

choices.text: An error, because the original was changed after a proxy was made of it
choices.why: Changing the original is ordinary JavaScript and raises nothing. That silence is the trap.

prompt: In the second `ReactiveProxy` run, a third click went through the proxy and the page jumped from 40 to 60. Why 60 and not 50?
hint: What was inside the object before the third click?

choices.text: The proxy queued the change made through the original and replayed it on the next write
choices.why: No change was recorded. The proxy reads and writes the same object, which already held 50.

choices.text: The third click added 20, to make up for the one that was missed
choices.why: `viaProxy` adds 10 every time; it knows nothing about the earlier click.

choices.text: `raw` became reactive once a proxy existed
choices.why: `isReactive(raw)` printed `false`. Making a proxy does not change the object it wraps.

choices.text: The object already held 50, because the second click changed it, and the redraw showed what it held
choices.why: Right. The change behind Vue's back was never lost, only unseen until something else caused a redraw.

prompt: Which of these can `reactive()` make reactive? Choose all that apply.
hint: The demo tried one that cannot, and Vue warned.

choices.text: A Map
choices.why: Right. Objects, arrays, Maps and Sets are what a Proxy can stand in for.

choices.text: The number 25
choices.why: The demo logged `value cannot be made reactive: 25` and handed the number back. A number has no properties to watch; that is what `ref` is for.

choices.text: An array of sessions
choices.why: Right. An array is an object, and its reads and writes go through the proxy.

choices.text: A plain object such as `{ course: 'spanish' }`
choices.why: Right. That is the case the demo built.

prompt: `isReactive(session.tags)` printed `true`, although `tags` was a plain array in `raw`. What does that show?
hint: The array was reached through something.

choices.text: `reactive()` copied the whole object, arrays included, when it was called
choices.why: Nothing was copied: `isReactive(raw)` stayed `false` and the proxy reads the original. The nested proxy is made when it is read.

choices.text: Arrays are reactive in Vue by default
choices.why: `raw.tags` is the same array, and it is not reactive. What made the difference is the path it was read through.

choices.text: `tags` was turned into a ref
choices.why: It is read as `session.tags` with no `.value`. Inside `reactive`, it is a proxy rather than a ref.

choices.text: Reading a nested object through a proxy returns a proxy of it
choices.why: Right. That is what deep means here: however far down a change is made, the path to it went through a proxy.

prompt: In `LostReactivity`, `week.done` went from 75 to 95. What did the line `destructured: {{ done }}` show after the click?
hint: `const { done } = week` ran once, in the setup.

choices.text: 95, a moment after the click
choices.why: That is how the update queue looks, but there is nothing to catch up: `done` is a plain number, and nothing will redraw it to 95.
That is the `toRefs` line. Destructuring the proxy itself took a copy of the number.
Right. Destructuring read `week.done` once and put the number in a new variable, and a number cannot report a change.

choices.text: Nothing, and a warning that a reactive object was destructured
choices.why: Vue gives no warning, because taking a value out of an object is ordinary JavaScript. The page showed a number, the wrong one.

prompt: `const { done } = week` takes a copy. To get a single ref that stays linked to that property instead, write `___(week, 'done')`.
hint: The singular of the function that does it for every property.

prompt: A component declares `let week = reactive({ planned: 0, done: 0 })`, and when the data arrives runs `week = reactive(loaded)`. What does the page show?
hint: Which proxy does the template hold?

choices.text: The loaded data, once the update queue has run
choices.why: The queue reruns renders that read a value that changed. Nothing the template read changed: it still holds the first proxy.

choices.text: The zeros of the first object
choices.why: Right. Pointing the variable at a second proxy changes nothing on the screen. A `ref` and `week.value = loaded` is the fix.

choices.text: An error, because a reactive variable is a constant
choices.why: It was declared with `let`, so the assignment is legal JavaScript. Nothing complains, which is why it slips through.

choices.text: The loaded data, and the old proxy is thrown away
choices.why: The template was compiled against the first proxy and keeps it; the second is one nobody watches.

prompt: The script has `const left = minutesLeft(week.goal, week.done)` and the template shows `{{ left }}`. When `week.done` changes, `left` stays. What is the fix the lesson gives?
hint: A value that has to be recomputed whenever its inputs change.

choices.text: `await nextTick()` before reading `left`
choices.why: `nextTick` waits for the page to catch up. It does not recompute a number that was taken once.

choices.text: Wrap the result: `const left = ref(minutesLeft(week.goal, week.done))`
choices.why: That makes a ref holding the first answer. Nothing writes to it when `week.done` changes, so it stays.

choices.text: `computed(() => minutesLeft(week.goal, week.done))`
choices.why: Right. The reads happen inside the `computed`, so they are tracked and it recomputes. Lesson 3 is about it.

choices.text: Destructure first: `const { goal, done } = toRefs(week)` and pass those
choices.why: The function would receive refs and subtract wrappers. It also still runs once; the call itself is what needs to be repeated.

prompt: `addThree` changed `count` three times in a row. How many times was `render with count = 3` logged?
hint: The writes queue redraws.

prompt: Inside `addThree`, right after the three increments, the code reads the `<output>`. What did it find, and why?
hint: Look at the line that starts `count is 3`.

choices.text: 1, because the first write redrew the page and the other two waited
choices.why: No write redrew the page on the spot. All three were queued into one redraw that ran after the function paused.

choices.text: 3, because each write redraws at once
choices.why: That is the common picture, and the transcript refutes it: `the page still says 0`.

choices.text: Nothing yet, because the `<output>` is drawn only after `nextTick`
choices.why: The output was drawn on the first render with 0; it is waiting to be redrawn, not to exist.

choices.text: 0, because the redraw is queued and waits for the code that changed `count` to finish
choices.why: Right. The value was 3 and the page still said 0; the queue runs as a microtask once the current code is done.

prompt: A colleague's total is wrong for a moment after each change, so they `await nextTick()` before computing it from the DOM. What does the lesson say this signals?
hint: `nextTick` is about the page, not about values.

choices.text: The total is computed in the wrong place, and belongs in `computed`
choices.why: Right. A `computed` is never stale. `nextTick` is for touching the DOM after a change, such as focusing a field that just appeared.

choices.text: Nothing wrong: this is what `nextTick` is for
choices.why: Waiting for the page and then reading a value off it puts a value where the DOM is the source. The lesson keeps `nextTick` for work on the DOM itself.

choices.text: The update queue is broken and has to be flushed by hand
choices.why: The queue did what it does: one redraw after the code finished. There is nothing to flush.

choices.text: The changes should be made with `reactive` instead of `ref`
choices.why: Both queue their redraws the same way. Which wrapper holds the value does not change when the page catches up.

prompt: With `public/courses.json` moved away, the page said `Unexpected token '<', "<!DOCTYPE "... is not valid JSON`. What happened?
hint: `curl -si` showed the reply's first lines.

choices.text: The file was found but had a stray `<` in it
choices.why: There was no file at all. The `<` starts the HTML of a page.

choices.text: The server answered 404, and `fetch` turned it into a JSON error
choices.why: A 404 would have failed the `response.ok` check with its own message. `curl` showed `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`.

choices.text: The request got the application's HTML page, with a 200
choices.why: Right. Vite answers an address it does not have with the page, so `response.ok` was true and `response.json()` failed on the first `<`.

choices.text: Vite had not started yet, and answered with its loading screen
choices.why: The dev server was running and served the rest of the page; it answered this address with the application, as it does for anything unknown.

prompt: Why does the planner's header have a `Loading…` state at all?
hint: When does the request start, and what is drawn before it ends?

choices.text: Vite shows it on its own while modules load
choices.why: The paragraph is in `App.vue`, chosen by `v-else-if="courses.length === 0"`. Vite draws nothing of the page.

choices.text: The refs start empty and the page is drawn before the file arrives
choices.why: Right. The setup starts the request and the template draws what the refs hold, an empty list, until the data replaces it.

choices.text: `fetch` blocks the component until the file is read, and the paragraph covers that pause
choices.why: `fetch` does not block anything. The component is drawn at once, which is why there is a state to draw.

choices.text: Every `ref` is shown as loading until its first write
choices.why: A ref has no loading state. The template decides what an empty list means.

prompt: The data arrives and the code runs `courses.value = data.courses`. Why does the list appear, though the template was drawn while `courses` was empty?
hint: What did the template read the first time it was drawn?

choices.text: Assigning `.value` reruns every render that read `courses`
choices.why: Right. The template read `courses.value` without saying so, and replacing it redrew what depended on it.

choices.text: The `.then` calls tell Vue to draw the component again from the start
choices.why: Promises know nothing about Vue, and nothing is drawn again from the start: the setup runs once.

choices.text: `v-for` checks its array again on a timer
choices.why: There is no polling. The redraw happens because of the write, not because time passed.

choices.text: The browser replaces the empty `<ul>` when `fetch` resolves
choices.why: The browser does not connect a request to an element. Vue redrew the list because a ref the template read was written.

prompt: Put what happens when the planner opens in the order it happens.
items: The render that read `courses` runs again

prompt: Match each line of code to what it leaves you with.
hint: Each of them either reads through the wrapper or takes something out of it.

pairs.right: A ref linked to the proxy
A change the page has not seen

prompt: A component has `const goal = ref(180)` and `const doubled = goal.value * 2`, and the template shows `{{ goal }}` and `{{ doubled }}`. A button sets `goal.value = 200`. After the redraw, what does the page show?
hint: One of the two names is a ref; the other was computed from one, once.

choices.why: That would need `doubled` to be a `computed`. As written, it is a number taken once in the setup.

choices.text: 180 and 360, because the template unwraps refs only on the first draw
choices.why: The template reads `goal` on every render, and the write to `goal.value` reruns it, so `goal` shows 200.
Right. `goal` is read through the wrapper at render time; `doubled` is a plain number that the setup computed once.

choices.text: 200 and `[object Object]2`
choices.why: `goal.value` is the number 180, so `goal.value * 2` is 360. The wrapper meets an operator only when `.value` is left out.

prompt: `week` is a `reactive` object. Which of these show the current `week.done` after it changes? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read through the wrapper at the last moment.

choices.text: `{{ week.done }}` in the template
choices.why: Right. The template reads through the proxy on every render, so the read is tracked.

choices.text: `const shown = week.done` in the script, then `{{ shown }}`
choices.why: That reads early, into a plain variable, and holds a copy of the number.

choices.text: `const left = computed(() => week.goal - week.done)`, then `{{ left }}`
choices.why: Right. The read happens inside the `computed`, which recomputes when `week.done` changes.

choices.text: `const { done } = toRefs(week)`, then `{{ done }}`
choices.why: Right. Each piece is a ref linked to the proxy's property.
